prize_parts.citation: for the conception and long-term leadership of the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos
for the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep the two-part configuration, but after the first round I hold it with a clearer view of what each part needs. B022 is the best-supported and cleanest-credited candidate on the table. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice and Ye's work taking it to 10^-18, with many-body clock control, are traceable to two people, reproduced in several laboratories and compared across them, and used for tests of constants, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter searches. Four of eight members put it in their preferred configuration, and every member who argues against it does so on thematic overlap with 2005 and 2012, not on the quality of the result. B002 is the second part because IceCube is a new observational window: a diffuse TeV-PeV astrophysical flux established in independent analysis channels, then the TXS 0506+056 association. The two parts are scientifically unrelated, so the prize is not a thin single-theme award, and together they use exactly three names. I looked hard at the alternative of B028 as the second part. Because B028 has three credited names, it cannot be combined with B022 under the three-person limit. The real choice is therefore B022 alone, B028 alone, or B022 with B002. I prefer the last because it recognises two mature achievements without the interpretive risk that four members themselves acknowledge for twisted bilayer graphene.
statement.case_against: The weak point is still B002 attribution. Four members (Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and, in part, Danielsson) have said that one name for a collaboration of hundreds needs a stated principle, and I have not heard an argument in the first round that fully supplies one. The best I can offer is that Halzen conceived the cubic-kilometre detector, led the construction from the AMANDA stage and led the programme through the diffuse-flux discovery. That is a defensible conceiver-and-leader claim, but it leaves out AMANDA-era contributors and the analysis leads, and it is weaker than the two-name pairing for B022. If the committee concludes it cannot defend that principle, I would not hold the prize hostage to it. B022 alone would then be my fallback, ahead of B028. A second reservation is that I cannot independently weigh B002 because it is in my own field, and the chair should not be the sole advocate of a candidate in his own area. On B022, the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real and the citation must name the lattice clock explicitly so it does not read as a third clock prize.

responses.point: Kroll holds B022 alone, stressing the clean two-name attribution and independent reproduction, doubting B002 because a single name for a collaboration discovery is harder to defend, and saying source identification in neutrino astronomy is incomplete.
responses.response: I agree on B022 and I have moved closer to your position on timing: the redefinition of the second is a metrological decision and I would not cite it. I also accept that individual source identifications are statistically modest. But the case for B002 does not rest on them. The diffuse flux was established independently in several channels, and that alone is a discovery. Where we differ is whether the attribution problem is disqualifying. I think it is a real cost, not a bar, and I would drop B002 if no principle can be agreed. I do not see the need to fill the second part with something weaker, so B022 alone is acceptable to me as a fallback.

responses.point: Lindroth declines to pair B022 with B002 now because the pairing would be driven by overlapping support, not a joint argument, and says she would revisit it if colleagues show that Halzen's conceptual role is decisive.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge and I will answer it as the joint argument she asked for. Both parts are measurement-driven achievements that opened a capability that did not exist: a lattice clock at 10^-18, and a km3 detector that turned high-energy neutrinos into an observable sky. The pairing is not a compromise but a choice of two unrelated advances, and it is limited by the three-name rule to one person for IceCube. On Halzen's decisive role I can only say that he proposed the instrument, led the programme from AMANDA onward and led the discovery paper; I cannot show it from the supplied record to the standard you want. If you and others judge that insufficient, I would accept B022 alone over a pairing you cannot support.

responses.point: Olsson now puts B028 first, arguing it is a concrete prediction-plus-observation discovery with broad support, and accepts that the unresolved pairing mechanism and the omission of Cao and the Dean group are costs, while sharing hesitation about a one-name B002.
responses.response: I take the breadth of support for B028 seriously; it is the one candidate everyone ranked and I placed it fourth. My hesitation is maturity, which you and Eriksson, Mehlig and Johansson each acknowledge: the experiments date from 2018 and the central phase is still without an agreed mechanism. A citation limited to flat bands and correlated phases would be defensible, and I would not oppose it, which is why it is my first alternative. But with the first-author team and the Dean group outside any three names, I would rather wait than fix a narrative the field is still revising. On your hesitation about Halzen, we agree on the problem, and I have said above that it is the weakest part of my configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B003 to B028, arguing it is the one candidate on all eight ballots, with a sharp quantitative prediction followed by observation, and holds that B022 is an alternative, with a view that it is more technological than conceptual.
responses.response: Breadth of ranking is evidence, but I do not treat a support count as a substitute for scientific judgment. On your point that the lattice clock is more technological than conceptual, I disagree on the facts: the magic-wavelength condition is a conceptual step, since it makes the trapping potential invisible to the clock transition, and it produced a several-order-of-magnitude gain that changed what could be measured. That is closer to the prize's long tradition of precision-measurement awards than to an incremental refinement. I agree with you that the unresolved superconductivity should not alone decide B028, and I would be comfortable with it if the committee prefers it, but I would still rank it second to the clock on maturity.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B037 to the pairing of B002 and B022, would keep the Galactic-plane result out of any IceCube citation as too recent, and holds B037 and B028 as alternatives.
responses.response: We now share a configuration, so I should say where I am more cautious. I agree the Galactic-plane result should not appear in the citation, and I will remove it. I limit the B002 citation to the conception and leadership of IceCube and the diffuse high-energy flux. I also want to be clear that agreement between the two of us is not independent evidence, since we both work close to particle and astroparticle physics, and it should not be counted as support for B002 beyond what the others have conceded. On B037 you are right that the Higgs observation is first-rate, but I still do not see an agreed principle for crediting detector architects, which keeps it as my second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether a single named laureate for B002 can be defended, given that IceCube is a collaboration-scale discovery and the credit list cannot be extended. If not, I would fall back to B022 alone.
Whether the committee judges B022 distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on frequency combs and ion clocks, and whether the citation wording is sufficient.
Whether B028 is mature enough without an agreed superconducting mechanism, and whether a citation limited to flat bands and correlated phases would settle that for the members who hold it first.
Whether Katori's lattice concept and Ye's accuracy work are fairly captured by two names, given uncredited contributors such as Lemonde.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile lists PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur ties and I work in astroparticle physics at KTH. None is a documented tie to IceCube or Halzen, but B002 is in my own field, which I have said above and which colleagues should weigh when judging my advocacy for it. B033 is close to my gamma-ray work and is not in my configuration. As chair I have not seen a reason to recuse from any shortlisted candidate. I do not know of any other tie from my profile.
